WHY THE SHIFT? Uncertain courts, certain revenue 1 Courts are split. India's Delhi HC saw training as likely fair dealing for "research"; a US appeals court rejected fair use for a legal-AI tool in Thomson Reuters v. ROSS. 2 Litigation is slow and costly. A deal brings money, attribution and traffic now. 3 Lawsuits create leverage. Publishers that can credibly sue negotiate better terms. ! Smaller publishers get left out. Without bargaining power, they may get neither a deal nor a day in court. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 04 / 08

10 clauses that matter 1 Scope of use Separate rights for training, real-time retrieval and display. Licensing one is not licensing all. 2 Excerpt limits Maximum length, no full-text reproduction, paywalled content respected. 3 Attribution & links How prominent the credit is, and a working link to the original. 4 Misattribution fixes Fast correction when AI invents stories in your name (ANI alleged exactly this). 5 Payment & audit Flat fee or usage-based, with usage reports and audit rights. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 05 / 08

10 clauses that matter 6 Exit & deletion What happens to content on termination, including content already used in trained models. 7 Release of past claims Does signing waive claims for past scraping? Draft this carefully, or say no explicitly. 8 Exclusivity & MFN Can you license rivals? Do you get terms as good as other publishers? 9 Personal data Archives contain personal data; DPDP duties and takedown routes must be allocated. 10 Law & forum Indian law and an Indian seat for disputes, not just the AI company's home courts. TA K E AWAY The next AI copyright battles will be fought in contracts. Until the law settles, the licence is the law between publisher and AI company. Getting scope, attribution, exit and past-claims clauses right matters as much as winning in court. Adv.
